Subject: Post-call: Redwood integration & schema questions

Thanks again for the call today — really appreciate the walkthrough of your use cases. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we have alignment: 

- Scope: server-side inference for Acme search assistant (query -> retrieve -> rerank -> structured output for UI).
- SDK & Auth: you indicated prefer server-side SDK & managed credentials (no browser keys). We'll recommend service-API-key for initial PoC; we can outline an IAM/assume-role flow for longer-term private deployments.
- Endpoints: recommend Redwood chat endpoint with structured output/tool-calling for the response schema (rather than raw completions) so you get JSON-first responses for downstream UI.
- Embeddings / Reranker: embeddings for retrieval (FAISS/DB) + lightweight reranker via Redwood rerank endpoint for top-K.

Open questions we flagged on the call (please confirm):
1) Expected max output size (rough token count) for the UI card?
2) Do you need streaming (token-by-token) to start rendering, or is non-streaming fine?
3) Any hard stop sequences we need for output JSON?

Next steps:
- I attached a short SDK setup guide and a sample response schema (see attachments).
- Ben will follow up with a recommended embeddings / rerank config.
- If you can confirm expected token sizes and streaming preference, we'll provision a sandbox API key and send a mutual action plan.

Attachments: redwood-sdk-setup.md (text/markdown), sample_schema.json (application/json), acme-mutual-action-plan.docx (application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document)

Best,

Thanks Marissa — great summary. A few clarifying Qs from our engineering side: 

- Auth / infra: For PoC we'll be fine with an API key on our backend. For longer term we may want to use an AWS IAM-based flow or VPC connector (we're on AWS). Can you share recommended patterns for private deployment auth (assume-role / short-lived creds) vs hosted API keys?

- Chat vs Completions: We want the model to return strict JSON (fields: title, summary, actions[]). Is the chat endpoint with structured-tool-calling the right approach, or should we use completions with a strict prompt + stop tokens? Which gives better reliability for strictly-structured JSON?

- Tokenization / max_tokens: Our UI expects up to ~300 words in the summary. What's the recommended max_tokens setting and how do tokenization differences (e.g. GPT-style tokenizers) map to our word estimate?

- Streaming: We prefer progressive render for better perceived latency. How does Redwood handle streaming for structured JSON (is partial JSON streamed? do you send intermediate chunks, or only final well-formed JSON)?

- Reranker latency: for live search we need sub-150ms P95 for the reranker if possible. What are typical latencies for your rerank endpoint (on hosted vs dedicated), and recommendations to hit that target?

Also — can you paste a quick sample cURL or SDK call for the chat endpoint that returns a JSON schema? That will help our engineers start wiring up the UI.

Thanks,

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Ramos <alex.ramos@acme.com>, Priya Shah <priya@acme.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-07-31T11:20:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Post-call: Redwood integration & schema questions

Great questions — answers below. TL;DR: use chat+structured output (tool-calling) for strict JSON; streaming supported and we stream token deltas (see note). Auth patterns differ by deployment mode (hosted vs private).

1) Auth / infra:
- Hosted: short-term PoC: server-side API key is simplest. We recommend storing it in your secrets manager and rotating it regularly.
- Private / VPC / On-prem: support for customer-managed KMS + short-lived certs. Typical pattern is an onboarding step where we exchange an AWS IAM role assume-role token to mint short-lived keys for the control plane; we can share an assume-role example if you want.

2) Chat vs Completions for strict JSON:
- Recommend Chat endpoint with structured output/tool-calling. It's more robust than relying solely on stop tokens because the runtime understands a schema and validates/parses the model's response into JSON before returning (reduces malformed outputs). Completions + stop tokens can work but is brittle for nested objects.

3) Tokenization / max_tokens:
- Useful heuristic: 1 token ≈ 0.75 words in English (varies). For ~300 words, set max_output_tokens ≈ 400. We also recommend limiting context by trimming retrieval results to reduce prompt size.
- Redwood exposes a token_count helper in the SDK to estimate cost before sending the request.

4) Streaming semantics for structured JSON:
- We support streaming both for text and structured responses. For structured outputs, we stream model tokens as they are generated. In parallel, the runtime emits incremental parse events (partial JSON structure) but the safest UI behavior is to render progressive text and then replace with the final parsed JSON object on completion.
- If you need strictly valid JSON at each update, we recommend using the final parsed object once streaming completes; otherwise render token deltas and show a loading skeleton until the final parse event.

5) Stop sequences and safety:
- You can still set stop tokens, but when using structured outputs we recommend schema constraints + a final end-of-output marker. That reduces accidental truncation.

6) Reranker latency and recommended config:
- Hosted: typical rerank P50 ~ 40ms, P95 ~ 180–300ms depending on model size.
- Dedicated: with reserved capacity you can get P95 <150ms using a lightweight reranker model (we can configure a cross-encoder optimized for latency). Also consider a 2-step: embeddings retrieval (fast) + rerank top 50–100.

Example SDK snippet (Node):

const Redwood = require('@redwood/inference');
const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY });

const res = await client.chat.create({
  model: 'redwood-chat-medium',
  messages: [{ role: 'system', content: 'You are a structured JSON generator' }, { role: 'user', content: 'Generate JSON with title, summary, actions' }],
  response_schema: { // server-side schema declaration - validated by runtime
    type: 'object',
    properties: { title: { type: 'string' }, summary: { type: 'string' }, actions: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } } },
    required: ['title','summary']
  },
  max_output_tokens: 400,
  stream: true // set to false to receive final parsed object only
});

// res will be an async iterator if stream=true, otherwise a final parsed JSON object

Attachments: sample_schema.json contains the JSON schema we discussed. I attached an SDK quickstart (redwood-sdk-setup.md) and a mutual action plan draft.

Links: Dev guide: https://docs.redwood.ai/inference/structured-output (will email a private link with examples)

If helpful I can ask solutions engineering to produce an assume-role example for your infra team. Otherwise we can provision a sandbox key once you confirm streaming preference and approximate token target.

Best,
Marissa

Quick note on embeddings + rerank:
- Recommendation: use 1536-dim embeddings for best semantic fidelity unless your vector DB prefers a different size.
- Retrieval: retrieve top 100 candidates by vector similarity, then apply a reranker on top 50–100. That keeps recall high while bounding reranker cost.
- Reranker model: choose a small cross-encoder tuned for ranking (we can provide a 1–3B param option) for lower latency. If you need <150ms P95, deploy reranker on Dedicated capacity and use batch invocations where possible.

Also: if you're embedding long docs, chunking strategy matters — use ~200–300 token chunks with overlap 20–50 tokens.

Happy to jump on a short call with your infra team to map latency targets to config options.

—Ben
